Strong empirical results achieving 65-71% ASR@0.5 on InternVL-2.5-8B with minimal clean accuracy degradation (1-3%)

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored security vulnerability in VLMs for visual grounding with clear practical motivation in embodied AI systems
Novel input-aware trigger generation approach using text-conditional U-Net to handle open-vocabulary setting is well-designed and thoughtful
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three VLMs (InternVL-2.5-8B, Ferret-7B, LlaVA-1.5-7B), four datasets, with thorough ablations and transferability analysis
Theoretical guarantees (Propositions 1 and 2) provide formal rigor regarding existence and convergence of the attack
Demonstrates strong stealthiness with minimal clean accuracy degradation (1-3%) while achieving consistent ASR across diverse configurations
Thorough evaluation against multiple defense mechanisms showing robustness to existing defense strategies
weaknesses: Moderate attack success rates (30-71% ASR@0.5) substantially lower than traditional backdoor attacks (>95%), raising questions about practical threat level and reliability in real-world deployment scenarios

Strong white-box threat model requiring access to training data and model weights during fine-tuning limits real-world applicability; practical scenario of poisoning inference-time images requires control over input data or system compromise

Inadequate baseline comparisons: no direct comparison with adapted existing attacks; BadEncoder/TrojVLM comparison uses incompatible 'close-vocabulary' setting; no ablation against simpler trigger generation approaches

Theoretical analysis relies on unrealistic assumptions (universal approximation of finite-capacity networks, dataset separability, fixed sufficient trigger pattern) and lacks practical grounding; proofs are abstract without connecting to why the algorithm works empirically

Shallow defense evaluation with only three methods, most designed for classification not visual grounding; no defense mechanisms tailored to this attack; insufficient analysis of why or whether IAG is inherently robust

Limited analysis of attack mechanisms: trigger patterns in Figure 3 are visually difficult to interpret; no visualization of learned semantic patterns; hyperparameter β set empirically without ablation
Real-world experiments lack rigor: only qualitative examples in Figures 6-12 without success rate statistics; results may be cherry-picked; minimal details on real-world image performance
Transferability shows dataset specificity (50-54% for RefCocog vs. 60-65% for RefCoco) with insufficient analysis, limiting claimed threat generality

Incomplete ablations: no study of reconstruction loss weight sensitivity, no comparison of poison rate strategies, no U-Net architecture comparisons; 'w/o mixup' shows only 2% drop questioning its importance
Attack data generation is overly simplistic (random target/query selection); no comparison of data generation strategies or evidence this approach is optimal
Reproducibility concerns: U-Net architecture specifications sparse; code release promised but unverified; hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary without justification
No constructive solutions provided: paper identifies vulnerability but offers no defenses or mitigation strategies for VLM developers
Missing evaluation on diverse VLM architectures and scales (only 7-8B models tested; no larger or newer architectures); results generalizability unclear
Some overclaimed statements: ASR of 50-70% described as 'remarkable' despite being moderate; claims about 'fundamental security concern' not fully supported given strong threat assumptions

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation addressing an underexplored security vulnerability in VLMs for visual grounding tasks with clear practical implications for embodied AI and autonomous systems

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 VLMs, 4 datasets, with thorough ablations (Table 4), transferability studies (Table 5), defense evaluation, and real-world validation demonstrating consistent ASR@0.5 of 50-71%

Technically sound approach using text-conditional U-Net for semantic-guided trigger generation with principled joint training of trigger generator and VLM, including reconstruction loss for imperceptibility
Provides theoretical analysis with Propositions on existence and convergence, offering formal backing for the attack's feasibility within generative model framework
Robust attack performance with very low poison rates (1% achieving ~50% ASR) and strong resistance to existing defenses (Spectral Signature, Beatrix, PAR), indicating practical threat potential
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and detailed experimental documentation including hyperparameters, algorithms, and commitment to code release for reproducibility
weaknesses: Moderate attack success rates (50-71% ASR@0.5) are substantially lower than traditional backdoor attacks (~100%), limiting threat severity; theoretical explanation for this performance plateau is incomplete

Significant gap between theoretical analysis and practice: Proposition 1 relies on unrealistic assumptions (universal approximation, dataset separability, existence of unique trigger pattern ψ) that are neither empirically validated nor tightly connected to actual L_rec + L_LM objective; convergence proof doesn't explain observed performance limits

Imperceptibility claims lack rigorous validation: no human studies or perceptual metrics (LPIPS, SSIM, FID) provided; reconstruction loss L_rec is crude metric; visual artifacts visible in Figure 3; hyperparameter β=0.5 chosen empirically without ablation or justification

Limited defense analysis with only 3 simple methods tested; explanation for robustness ('dynamic patterns') is descriptive rather than mechanistic; no investigation of gradient masking or proposal of improved defenses

Experimental limitations: baseline comparisons use simplified adapted settings; poison rate only explored up to 10%; no systematic analysis of which object categories are easier/harder to attack; missing critical ablations on smooth L1 choice and β sensitivity

Generalization concerns: all experiments use LoRA fine-tuning; unclear how method transfers to full model tuning or frozen models; requires white-box training-time access, limiting real-world applicability; code unavailable at submission

Theoretical proof issues: gate function (Eq. A.1) is informal; assumptions in Lemmas 1-4 not empirically verified during training; convergence proof lacks rigorous connection to actual dynamics; unused assumptions like dataset separability not validated

Missing critical analyses: behavior when target object absent from image; effect of semantic similarity between query and target; cross-model transferability (trained on model A, tested on B); why RefCocog transfer degrades more (Table 5)

strengths: Novel and practical problem: First multi-target backdoor attack on VLM-based visual grounding, addressing a realistic threat where previous static-trigger attacks are unsuitable
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Five datasets, three VLM architectures, extensive ablations, defense evaluations, transferability analysis, and real-world examples
Strong empirical results: Achieves highest ASR in 11/12 settings (11.9%-32.8% improvement over baselines) while maintaining <3% benign accuracy drop and minimal inference overhead
Thorough imperceptibility analysis: PSNR 31-32 dB (above perceptual threshold), low L1/LPIPS scores, with visual demonstration of trigger naturalness
Well-executed presentation: Clear methodology, good visualizations, comprehensive supplementary material with hyperparameters and implementation details
Robustness against existing defenses: Demonstrates IAG evades Spectral Signature, Beatrix, PAR, and adaptive defenses
Practical effectiveness: Attack remains effective at 1% poison rate, demonstrating efficiency
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Text-conditioned UNet is from existing diffusion models; joint loss combining reconstruction and LM loss is straightforward; primary contribution is application rather than methodological innovation
Weak theoretical analysis: Assumptions A1-A3 lack empirical validation; bounds are loose; no proof that assumptions actually hold; informal explanation of why input-aware triggers help
Significant performance gaps on complex tasks: ShowUI ASR only 25-35%, COCO-2017 ASR 40-47%, limiting practical threat credibility despite justification about unseen objects

Incomplete baseline comparison: Most baselines adapted from classification tasks; VLM-specific baselines (BadVLMDriver, TrojVLM, VLOOD) achieving 42-48% ASR relegated to Appendix J, contradicting main paper dismissal of 'ASR ≈ 0'
Mixed transferability results: RefCoco→RefCocog transfer shows significant drop (50.2%→60.3%), suggesting limited robustness to distribution shift; VQA transfer uses ethically problematic hate speech
No proposed defenses or mitigations: Thoroughly critiques attacks but offers no solutions or future defense directions, limiting constructive impact for security research

Hyperparameter selection inadequately justified: β=0.5 chosen despite Table 9 showing β=0.1 achieves slightly higher ASR; α₁, α₂ follow general recommendations without dataset-specific validation; max token lengths appear ad-hoc
Limited failure case analysis: No systematic investigation of which object types are harder to attack, or how ASR correlates with object similarity to training targets

Real-world evaluation not systematic: Only example-based results; screenshots appear manually created rather than from live systems; no evaluation on actual GUI agents or embodied AI systems mentioned in motivation
Suspicious defense results: Table 4 shows Beatrix defense increases ASR (50.2%→54.2% on RefCocog), counter-intuitive result without explanation suggesting possible experimental issue

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine security vulnerability in VLM-based visual grounding that is timely and practically relevant
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple VLMs (LLaVA, InternVL, Ferret), datasets (RefCOCO variants, Flickr30k, ShowUI), and extensive ablations
Strong imperceptibility demonstration with PSNR 31-32 dB and LPIPS < 0.05, including attention map visualization
Extensive analysis including poison rate sensitivity (1-5%), transferability across datasets/tasks, time overhead, and real-world evaluation
Good motivation for using text-conditioned UNet with clear architectural justification over prior approaches (linear mappers, shallow autoencoders)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing text-conditioned diffusion architecture (Rombach et al., 2022) and standard backdoor training objectives without substantial adaptation or innovation
Moderate attack success rates (25-68%) undermine threat severity claims; ASRs don't approach 100% and fall below practical attack thresholds, especially on complex ShowUI dataset

Unfair baseline comparisons: One-to-N, Imperio, Marksman designed for classification/retrieval not VLM grounding; primary comparison methods not adapted for multi-target scenario; static-target VLM attacks relegated to appendix
Insufficient defense contribution: evaluates existing defenses not designed for this attack, shows they fail, but proposes no VLM-specific defenses or mitigation strategies

Unvalidated theoretical analysis: Proposition 1 relies on assumptions A1-A3 without empirical validation; A2 (local linearization) questionable for complex VLMs; proof is standard Taylor expansion with limited novel insight

Weak threat model: requires substantial attacker capabilities (finetune VLM, inject 5% poison ~850 images), assumes no deployment-time security practices; limited discussion of modern supply chain defenses

Methodological concerns: random attack target selection may introduce bias, fixed prompt template advantages IAG by design, no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, baseline reproduction details sparse

Missing failure analysis: insufficient explanation of 32-75% failure rate across datasets; limited investigation of systematic vulnerabilities (object categories, image characteristics) that affect attack success

strengths: Novel multi-target backdoor attack on VLM-based visual grounding—first work addressing this realistic scenario beyond static-trigger attacks
Technically sound approach using text-conditioned UNet with well-motivated joint optimization of reconstruction and language modeling losses
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 VLMs, 5 datasets, with extensive ablations, defense evaluations, transferability analysis, and real-world validation
Strong empirical results achieving highest ASR in 11/12 settings (11.9%-32.8% above baselines) while maintaining benign accuracy within 3% of clean models
Imperceptibility rigorously validated via PSNR (31-32 dB), LPIPS (<0.04), and L1 metrics that align with established perceptual standards
Theoretical analysis providing formal justification for input-aware triggers via margin lower bounds, explaining superiority over fixed triggers
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed architecture, hyperparameters, algorithms, and extensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Moderate attack success rates (25.7%-66.9%) with significant variance across datasets—far from 100% typical of backdoor attacks, limiting immediate practical threat level

Defense analysis insufficient: while showing existing defenses fail, paper proposes no countermeasures and lacks deep analysis of trade-offs (e.g., 15% clean accuracy drop vs 9% ASR drop for JPEG compression)
Theoretical framework (Section 3.6) makes strong assumptions (A1-A3) but provides no empirical validation—assumption A3 about target-aligned feature shift is particularly opaque and unverified

Limited analysis of attack failure modes: no investigation of which object/target characteristics lead to failure, and significant cross-dataset degradation (RefCoco→RefCocog: 66.9%→50.2%) lacks explanation
Weak cross-dataset transferability undermines generalization claims; transfer to RefCocog shows substantial performance drops but causes are unexplored
Trigger mechanism unexplained beyond attention visualization—what semantic content is encoded and how triggers interact with model internals remains unclear
Real-world evaluation limited to one detailed scenario (Case 1); more diverse applications and image types needed to support practical threat claims
Hyperparameter and design choices lack principled justification: 5% poison rate arbitrary, architecture ablations missing, token length selection (30/50) unjustified
